text:
Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with a fixed number of binary digits. For ordinary real arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding a and b first, then c, is equivalent to adding a to the sum of b and c. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result generally must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Changing the grouping changes which intermediate values are formed and therefore where rounding occurs.

The effect is especially visible when the operands have very different magnitudes. If a very small number is added to a very large number, the small contribution may lie below the precision available at the large number’s scale and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are combined first, their sum may become large enough to affect the larger operand. Cancellation also matters: adding nearly equal values with opposite signs can discard leading significant digits, making later rounding errors relatively important. Thus, even when each hardware operation follows the applicable floating-point standard correctly, different legal evaluation orders can produce slightly different answers.

A matrix multiplication consists of many dot products. Each output element is a sum of products, often involving thousands or millions of terms. High-performance implementations divide this work among vector lanes, processor cores, GPU threads, and distributed nodes. Those partial sums are then combined through a reduction tree. The tree’s shape depends on choices such as block size, thread scheduling, processor count, kernel implementation, and communication order. Because addition is not associative, two mathematically equivalent reduction trees need not produce bit-for-bit identical output.

The differences are usually small, often only a few units in the last place, but they can accumulate or be amplified by ill-conditioned calculations and subsequent nonlinear operations. Fused multiply-add instructions can introduce another variation: computing a product and addition with one final rounding is generally more accurate, but it may differ from executing separate multiplication and addition instructions with two roundings. Different hardware or compiler settings may therefore change results even when the source algorithm is unchanged.

Reproducibility requires controlling these choices. Using a fixed reduction order, identical kernels and hardware features, deterministic scheduling, and consistent compiler options can make repeated runs bitwise stable. More specialized approaches use compensated summation, wider accumulators, or reproducible reduction algorithms. These techniques can improve accuracy or determinism, but often cost performance, memory, or parallel scalability. Consequently, large matrix multiplications are commonly expected to agree within a numerical tolerance rather than match bit for bit across execution configurations.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing parentheses does not change a sum: adding a and b first, then c, gives the same result as adding b and c first, then a. A floating-point processor, however, usually rounds the result of each operation to the nearest representable value. Because rounding occurs after intermediate additions, changing their order changes which values are rounded and when, potentially changing the final result.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. If a small number is added to a much larger number, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear entirely. If several small numbers are added together first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the larger number. Cancellation also matters: subtracting nearly equal values can discard many significant digits, making later rounding errors comparatively important. IEEE 754 defines floating-point formats and common rounding behavior, but it does not make rounded addition associative.

Large matrix multiplication exposes this issue because every output element is a dot product, hence a reduction of many products. High-performance implementations do not generally accumulate those products in a single fixed left-to-right order. They divide matrices into tiles, distribute work across processor cores or accelerators, form partial sums, and combine those sums through reduction trees. Different thread schedules, tile sizes, vector widths, processor counts, compiler optimizations, or GPU kernels can therefore produce different reduction orders. Some systems may also use fused multiply-add instructions, which round a multiplication and addition only once, while others may perform and round the two operations separately.

Consequently, two mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications can produce results that differ in their least significant bits. For well-conditioned calculations, these discrepancies are usually tiny and remain within an appropriate numerical tolerance. They can nevertheless grow through subsequent operations, particularly in ill-conditioned problems, iterative algorithms, or computations involving extensive cancellation. Parallel execution may even vary from run to run if the order in which partial results arrive is nondeterministic.

Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same input data. It typically requires a fixed reduction order, consistent instruction choices and precision, controlled compiler behavior, and deterministic parallel scheduling. Such constraints can reduce performance because they limit scheduling freedom and may prevent use of the fastest architecture-specific kernels. Numerical software commonly favors reproducibility within a tolerance rather than identical bit patterns, while applications requiring exact repeatability must deliberately select deterministic algorithms or reproducible summation techniques.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding the first two values and then the third is equivalent to adding the last two values first. Floating-point hardware, however, must round most intermediate results to the nearest representable number. Because each grouping produces different intermediate values, rounding can occur at different points and in different directions, leading to different final answers.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. Suppose a large value is combined with a much smaller value. The smaller value may fall below the precision available at the scale of the larger one and disappear during rounding. If several small values are added together first, they may accumulate into a quantity large enough to affect the eventual sum. If each is added separately to the large value, their contributions may be lost. Cancellation between nearly equal values can also magnify the influence of earlier rounding errors.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products, each of which reduces a sequence of products into a sum. High-performance implementations divide this work across vector lanes, processor cores, GPU threads, or distributed machines. Partial sums may be formed in blocks and then combined through a reduction tree. Changing the block size, thread count, scheduling, tiling strategy, hardware architecture, or library implementation can therefore change the reduction order. Although all implementations evaluate the same mathematical expression, they need not produce bit-for-bit identical floating-point results.

Fused multiply-add instructions introduce another source of variation. They compute a multiplication and addition with a single final rounding, whereas separate instructions normally round the product before performing the addition. Fused operations are usually more accurate, but a program using them can differ from one that does not. Compilers and numerical libraries may also rearrange operations when aggressive optimization modes permit it.

For a large matrix multiplication, each individual discrepancy is generally tiny, often only a few units in the last place. Across long reductions, however, these differences can accumulate. The result is usually numerically close but not exactly reproducible across runs, machines, or parallel configurations. In sensitive downstream calculations, small discrepancies may be amplified. Achieving strict reproducibility requires fixing the reduction order and arithmetic behavior, or using techniques such as compensated, pairwise, or higher-precision summation. Those choices typically impose costs in speed, memory use, or parallel scalability, so numerical software often favors bounded accuracy over bitwise identity.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of a sum does not change its value: adding a to b first and then c gives the same result as adding a to the sum of b and c. A floating-point processor, however, usually rounds the result of each operation to the nearest representable number. Because rounding occurs after intermediate additions, changing their order changes which intermediate values are rounded and can therefore change the final result.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes or when positive and negative terms nearly cancel. If a very small value is added to a much larger one, the smaller contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear entirely. If several small values are added together first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the later addition. Similarly, cancellation can discard leading significant digits and magnify the relative importance of rounding errors introduced earlier. IEEE 754 specifies floating-point formats and many details of individual operations, but it does not make differently ordered sequences of operations mathematically equivalent. Additional hardware behavior, such as fused multiply-add instructions, extended intermediate precision, and compiler transformations, can also alter where rounding occurs.

Each entry of a matrix product is a dot product: a sequence of multiplications followed by a reduction that adds the products. Large matrix-multiplication implementations divide this work across vector lanes, processor cores, GPU threads, or distributed machines. For performance, partial sums may be accumulated in trees, tiles, or blocks rather than strictly from left to right. The precise order can depend on the algorithm, thread scheduling, tile size, device architecture, library version, or number of workers. Two executions that use different reduction orders may therefore produce results that differ by a few units in the last place, even though both correctly approximate the same exact matrix product.

These small discrepancies can propagate through later computations. In numerically stable applications they may remain insignificant, but iterative algorithms, threshold decisions, chaotic simulations, or poorly conditioned problems can amplify them into visible differences. Consequently, mathematical reproducibility does not automatically imply bitwise reproducibility. Achieving identical results across reduction orders generally requires imposing a deterministic order or using special reproducible summation techniques, often at a cost in speed, memory traffic, or parallel scalability. Tolerance-based comparisons and numerical error analysis are therefore usually more appropriate than expecting exact equality between large matrix products computed on different hardware or with different parallel configurations.

In exact arithmetic, changing parentheses does not change a sum: adding a and b first, then c, gives the same result as adding b and c first, then a. In floating-point arithmetic, however, most intermediate results cannot be represented exactly. After each operation, the hardware rounds the exact result to the nearest representable value, according to the active rounding mode. Different parenthesizations create different intermediate values, so rounding occurs at different points and can produce different final answers.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes or when positive and negative terms nearly cancel. If a small number is added to a much larger one, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear during rounding. If the small values are combined first, their accumulated contribution may become large enough to survive when later added to the larger value. Cancellation can also discard significant digits and magnify the influence of subsequent rounding. IEEE 754 specifies floating-point formats and operation semantics carefully, but it does not make rounded addition associative. Hardware features such as fused multiply-add may further alter intermediate rounding by performing a multiplication and addition with only one final rounding rather than two.

Large matrix multiplications expose this issue because every output element is a dot product containing many products that must be summed. High-performance implementations rarely accumulate these products in one fixed left-to-right sequence. They divide matrices into tiles, distribute work among processor cores or accelerators, and combine partial sums through reduction trees. Changing the tile size, thread count, scheduling, vector width, GPU kernel, compiler options, or device architecture can change the reduction order. Although every order is mathematically equivalent over real numbers, it may follow a different sequence of floating-point roundings.

Consequently, two correct executions can produce matrices whose entries differ by a few units in the last place. For long dot products, poorly conditioned problems, or extensive cancellation, discrepancies can be larger and may propagate through later computations. Parallel scheduling can even make repeated runs on the same system differ if partial results are combined nondeterministically.

Reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same input values. Bitwise-identical results generally require a fixed reduction order, consistent floating-point formats and instructions, and controlled compiler and library behavior. Deterministic reductions, compensated summation, higher-precision accumulation, or exact reproducible accumulators can reduce or eliminate variation, but they often cost performance, memory, or portability. In practice, numerical software commonly tests results with tolerances rather than demanding exact equality, while applications needing strict reproducibility deliberately constrain execution and accumulation methods.

In floating-point arithmetic, however, the exact result of each addition is usually rounded to the nearest representable value. Since rounding occurs after every operation, different groupings create different intermediate values and therefore can produce different final answers.

If a very small number is added to a much larger one, the small contribution may lie below the precision available near the larger number and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are combined first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the later addition. Cancellation also matters: adding nearly equal values with opposite signs can erase leading digits, magnifying the influence of earlier rounding errors. Consequently, even hardware that follows the IEEE 754 standard can legitimately return slightly different sums when operations are reordered. Fused multiply-add instructions, extended intermediate precision, subnormal-number handling, and compiler optimizations may introduce further differences across processors or execution modes.

A matrix multiplication computes each output entry as a dot product, which is a sum of many products. Large implementations do not normally accumulate those products in one fixed left-to-right sequence. They divide matrices into tiles and distribute work among vector lanes, CPU threads, GPU warps, or multiple machines. Partial sums are then combined through a reduction tree. Changing tile sizes, thread scheduling, device counts, library versions, or algorithms can change that tree. Because addition is not associative, each reduction order follows a slightly different path of intermediate rounding and may produce a different low-order bit pattern.

These discrepancies are usually tiny relative to the scale of the result, but they can grow with long reductions or poorly conditioned calculations. They may also become visible when later operations amplify small perturbations, or when programs make threshold decisions, compare results bit for bit, or train iterative machine-learning models whose trajectories diverge over time.

Thus, mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications need not be bitwise reproducible. Reproducibility generally requires fixing the algorithm and reduction order, controlling hardware and compiler behavior, or using specialized reproducible summation methods. Higher precision, pairwise summation, and compensation can reduce error, but they do not automatically guarantee identical results unless the complete execution order and arithmetic semantics are also constrained.
